title: Modules, Packages, and Imports
description: Structure your codebase into modular files, packages, and master import mechanisms.

blocks.content: As software scales beyond a single script, putting thousands of lines into one file is impossible to maintain. Python allows you to split code across multiple **Modules** (single `.py` files) and group them into **Packages** (directories containing an `__init__.py` file).

## Standard Built-in Modules

Python includes a rich "batteries-included" standard library:

```python
import json
import random
from datetime import datetime, timezone

# JSON serialization
data = {"user": "Alice", "score": 100}
json_str = json.dumps(data)

# Random generation
roll = random.randint(1, 6)

# Timestamps
now = datetime.now(timezone.utc).isoformat()
print(f"Rolled: {roll} at {now}")
```

## The `if __name__ == '__main__':` Idiom

When a file is run directly (e.g. `python app.py`), Python sets the special variable `__name__` to `'__main__'`. When the file is imported by another script (`import app`), `__name__` is set to `'app'`.

```python
def start_server():
    print("Server running on port 8000...")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    # Only runs when executed directly, NOT when imported!
    start_server()
```

```mermaid
graph TD
    A["python app.py"] -->|__name__ == '__main__'| B["Runs startup script"]
    C["import app"] -->|__name__ == 'app'| D["Imports functions only (no execution)"]
```

blocks.question: What is the purpose of an `__init__.py` file inside a folder?
options: It tells Python to treat the directory as a package containing importable modules
It compiles all Python files into machine code
It runs an antivirus scan on every import
It disables all global variables in the folder
blocks.explanation: An `__init__.py` file (which can be empty) marks a directory as a regular Python package, enabling dot-notation imports like `import my_package.helpers`.
